opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think the core difference is that in 2016 the field was wide open in a way it just isn't anymore. When I started, deep learning was only beginning to touch robotics. You could take an idea that worked in vision, adapt it to a manipulation problem, run it on a single robot arm in the lab, and that would be a real contribution. The bar for novelty was lower because almost everything was unexplored, and a single student with one robot and a GPU or two could push the frontier.

Today, the frontier has moved toward scale. The most visible results come from large foundation models trained on huge amounts of robot data, collected across fleets of robots, sometimes by teams of dozens of engineers with serious compute budgets. A PhD student in an academic lab can't compete head-on with that, so the first hard problem is figuring out what research you can do that actually matters and won't be made obsolete in six months by an industry lab scaling things up.

The second thing is speed and noise. Back then you could read most of the important papers in robot learning in a few weeks. Now there are new papers and models every day, plus demos on social media that may or may not hold up. Just separating real progress from hype takes a lot of judgment, and students are expected to have that judgment very early.

Third, expectations have gone up. Because there's so much attention and money in robotics now, students feel pressure to show impressive real-world demos, generalist behavior, and lots of evaluation, not just a clean idea in simulation. That's good for the field, but it's a heavy load for one person.

That said, I don't think it's all bad news. The tools are far better, hardware is cheaper, and there are open datasets and models students can build on. The opportunity is still huge, but you have to be much more deliberate. Pick problems where academia has a real advantage: understanding why things work, new ways to get data, evaluation, safety, human-robot interaction, or ideas that are too risky for industry to bet on. The students who do well now are the ones who think carefully about where they fit, rather than trying to win the scaling race.

r001.rationale: It describes the challenge of keeping up with papers and avoiding work made obsolete, but does not attribute difficulty to fear of falling behind specifically when disconnected from mainstream research.

r002.rationale: It says students need to be deliberate about where they fit and to choose problems where academia has an advantage, communicating the need to think through why a direction is worth pursuing.

r003.rationale: It gives reasons to favor directions such as evaluation or safety, and to avoid trying to win the scaling race, thereby comparing reasons for pursuing and rejecting research paths.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that the field got a lot more crowded and a lot more expensive at the same time, and those two things compound on each other.

Back around 2016, if you were a robotics PhD student, you could pick a fairly narrow problem, say grasping with a single arm, or visual servoing, and if you made a solid contribution with a modest setup and a few thousand trials, that was a respectable paper. The bar was clear. The number of people working on it was manageable. You knew most of the names in your subarea.

Now the frontier has shifted toward large-scale learning. The exciting results come from huge datasets, big models, lots of compute, and often fleets of robots collecting data. A single student with one arm and one workstation is competing against industry labs with hundreds of robots and effectively unlimited GPUs. So there's this constant anxiety of, what can I actually do in a five-year PhD that won't just be made obsolete by a scaling result six months from now?

There's also the pace. Students feel like they need to publish constantly, track every arXiv drop, and be visible on social media. In 2016 you could spend a year going deep on something and nobody thought you had disappeared. Today that feels risky, even though deep thinking is exactly what a PhD is supposed to train.

That said, I don't want to be purely pessimistic. I actually think there's a lot of room for students, because the big labs are optimizing for a specific kind of result. There are still enormous open questions about why these systems fail, how to get reliable long-horizon behavior, how to learn from very little data, how to integrate reasoning and physical interaction. Those are things that benefit from careful thinking more than from compute. The hard part is having the confidence to pick one of them and ignore the noise, and that's the part I try to help my students with the most.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes anxiety that a PhD project could be made obsolete by a scaling result, but does not attribute the difficulty to fear of being left behind when disconnected from mainstream research.

r002.rationale: It encourages careful thinking and choosing an open question, but does not say research taste develops by thinking through why a direction is worth pursuing.

r003.rationale: It advises picking a question and ignoring noise, but does not describe examining reasons to pursue or reject alternative research paths.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s harder in the sense that the field is moving so quickly, while a PhD still requires you to spend years developing a coherent research direction. You need to find a problem that matters today but will still matter when you finish. That’s a difficult bet to make in 2026.

Around 2016, you could often isolate a fairly specific robotics problem, develop a method, and demonstrate a meaningful advance with a relatively small setup. Today, your work may be compared with systems built using enormous datasets, substantial compute, and teams of engineers. So there’s a bigger gap between the resources available to an individual PhD student and the resources behind some of the strongest results.

And the physical part hasn’t gotten proportionally easier. Robots still break. Collecting data still takes time. You can have the software landscape change dramatically while you’re spending months getting an experiment to work reliably.

But I wouldn’t say that makes a robotics PhD less worthwhile. It makes choosing the right question more important. You want a question where your insight is the contribution, and where better models and better tools help you answer it rather than make it disappear.

r002.rationale: It says choosing the right question matters and that insight should be the contribution, but does not say developing research taste requires thinking through why a direction is worth pursuing.

r003.rationale: The response does not describe examining reasons for pursuing or rejecting alternative research paths.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the bar has moved a lot. Around 2016, you could take a fairly focused problem—say, learning a particular manipulation skill—and showing that it worked on a real robot could already be a meaningful contribution. The field had so many basic questions open.

Now, you’re expected to understand a much larger stack: robot hardware, control, perception, machine learning, large pretrained models, data collection. And the comparison point might be a system built by a company with a huge team and resources that a PhD student simply doesn’t have. So even figuring out what constitutes a compelling result becomes harder.

There’s also a timing problem. A PhD takes several years, but the tools and baselines can change while you’re working on your thesis. You have to ask, ‘Am I studying a fundamental problem, or am I solving something that the next model release might make irrelevant?’

That doesn’t mean there are fewer important questions. There are plenty. But choosing a question that’s important, tractable with academic resources, and durable enough to build a research direction around—that’s a much bigger part of the job now.

r002.rationale: It lists qualities of a good research question and asks whether work will remain relevant, but does not state that developing research taste requires thinking through why a direction is worth pursuing.
